title: What 'making it clearer' means
idea: MEET (thinking): refactoring is changing HOW code reads without changing WHAT it does. Same answers, friendlier code. No new syntax.

exercises.prompt: Your program already works and gives the right answers. 'Refactoring' means...
options: Making the code clearer and tidier WITHOUT changing what it does
Adding brand-new features
Making it give different answers
Deleting the whole thing and starting over
exercises.explanation: Refactoring = improving how code reads while keeping the behavior identical. Same inputs, same outputs - just easier to understand.

exercises.prompt: A good refactor can change the program's output.
exercises.explanation: No. If the output changed, you didn't refactor - you altered behavior. The golden rule: same answers before and after.

exercises.prompt: Why bother tidying code that already works?
options: Clear code is easier to read, fix, and reuse later - including by future you
The computer runs clear code faster, always
It is a rule the computer enforces
It changes the answer to be more correct
exercises.explanation: The computer doesn't care how pretty the code is. PEOPLE do. Clear code saves you time every time you come back to it.

exercises.prompt: Which of these count as refactoring (clarity, same behavior)? Pick ALL that apply.
options: Renaming a variable from x to total_price
Replacing three copy-pasted lines with one loop
Changing the discount from 10% to 20%
Pulling a repeated calculation into a helper function
exercises.explanation: Rename, de-duplicate, and extract-a-helper all keep behavior the same. Changing 10% to 20% changes the ANSWER - that's a feature change, not a refactor.

exercises.prompt: Before you refactor, what should you already have?
options: A correct, working solution you can re-check against
A brand-new problem to solve
An error you can't fix
Nothing - refactoring comes first
exercises.explanation: You tidy something that already works. The working version is your safety net: refactor, then re-run to prove the answers didn't change.

exercises.prompt: Match each tidy-up move to what it improves.

pairs.right: Fix a thing once, not in five places
Give a chunk of logic a clear name

exercises.explanation: These are the three main refactoring moves this unit practices. All three keep behavior identical.

exercises.prompt: Refactoring introduces new syntax you haven't learned yet.
exercises.explanation: No new syntax at all. You already know names, loops, and functions. Refactoring is about using them to make a solution READ better.

exercises.prompt: A friend reads your code and says 'what does p2 mean?' This is a sign that...
options: A better name would make the code clearer
The code is broken
You should add more variables named p3, p4
You need a faster computer
exercises.explanation: If a reader has to guess what a name means, the name is doing a poor job. A clear name like second_price answers the question for them.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best captures the spirit of refactoring?
options: Same result, clearer path
Different result, same path
More features, less testing
Faster to type, harder to read
exercises.explanation: Same result, clearer path. You keep the WHAT (the answers) and improve the HOW (the readability).

options: Taking a correct solution and making it clearer without breaking it
Learning a new loop
Solving a brand-new kind of problem
Speeding up the computer
exercises.explanation: Your first taste of refactoring: rename, de-duplicate, and extract helpers - all while the answers stay exactly the same.
